Viwe Jingqi: Addicted to Speed

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Addicted to Speed. 17 year old athlete Viwe Jingqi is driven by ambitions to write her family's name into South African history books, and it’s already happening.

Unique Selling Point:
Viwe Jingqi is shattering the hiatus in South African female track and field. From humble beginnings in rural Eastern Cape, Viwe is now in Grade 12 and has a bursary at Tuksport High School Pretoria. After shattering 4 South African youth records this month, she is to compete in the senior national championships this weekend. Viwe's coach Paul Gorries is eager to see how she handles the pressure of this step up in competition - and he believes she can win.

Summary:
Driven on with ambitions to write her family's name into South African history books, in April this year she broke 4 National sprinting records which were almost 40 years old. Her mother pushes her academically while her father (a sprinter too) supports her wholeheartedly in developing her talent on the track - a route he thinks can bring rewards for Viwe, which she wants to share with her family. Tragically her closest confidante and motivator, her older brother, died last year in a car crash - but he still drives her on.

Viwe says she always knew she was fast as she always outran boys and
girls in Engcobo Eastern Cape, now she knows an athletic career can give
her and her family the life they always wanted.

Treatment:
Pretoria: A day in the life of a star in the making, the pursuit of academic and athletic excellence – a filmic intimate story, getting into the head of Viwe, her philosophy and what drives this super talented South African - an inspirational story.
Cape Town: National Athletics meet – Viwe in action and watching on, her parents and coach Paul Gorries. . We can supplement with Super Sport footage of the event.

Further information:
Onwards and upwards. This is the start of Viwe's quest to ultimately challenge the fastest women on the planet. She knows it is going to take a lot of hard work and is not afraid to grind out her future on the track. She has the support of family, her coach and school behind her and the eternal motivation of her late brother Vukile. Viwe is philosophical about the journey her talent has started her on, identifying the root of her success, an addiction to speed: "If you had the opportunity to be as fast as I am, you would also be addicted. It's a great feeling."

Press Release:


From smashing the 100-metre sprint in under 20 seconds, to breaking a 40-year-old record… could 17-year-old South African athlete Viwe Jingqi become the next golden girl of world athletics?

Script:


Viwe: The last time I see people is before we go into the blocks. After that, I just switch on,

Viwe: It's me and my lane and the finish line.

Commentator: 100-meter, final women under 18. It's a terrific start this time around, and already quickly into her running is going to be Viwe Jingqi. Watch the clock, watch her run, Viwe Jingqi, remember the name. Cometh the hour, cometh the athlete.

LINK: Driven by ambitions to write her family's name into South African history books at this year's Junior championships, Viwe Jingqi smashed the 100-meter record three times//

Commentator: (the 200-meter race) Viwe Jingqi's flying away….
VO (over 200 m final):
And her 200-meter time of 23.03 seconds beat a record that was set 40 years ago to the day.
Commentator: She's taken this race out of orbit.

Sound up Viwe: You know I came here with only willing to break the 100-meter record but then miracles happened and I believe God is here for me.

Paul: Before we went to Potchefstroom, I already knew look, I mean, we're gonna see something special.

VO: Viwe's coach, former champion athlete Paul Gorries, has been nurturing this blossoming track and field athlete over the last two years.

Paul: I mean, those records stood for years. So that in itself should tell you, what caliber athlete you you're dealing with?

VO: Viwe had eclipsed the under 18 records for both sprints, remarkably her 11.22 seconds for the 100-metres was also an under 20 record.// At just seventeen this superstar in the making oozes confidence and when asked to describe herself, she doesn't hesitate.

Viwe: Smart is the first one, kind, talented, disciplined, and beautiful.
Claire: I agree with all of those five words. You are correct.

VO: But Viwe hasn't always been this self-assured - Born in rural Eastern Cape, her path to success was strewn with obstacles.

Viwe: I grew up there with mostly my mother because my father was working in another town.
Claire: At what point did you start running?
Viwe: I started in 2015. It was a small competition at school. I was 10 years, my coach told me that it's a great age to start running. He saw me running there. And he was like, Yeah, you could take this as something that can take you far.
VO: She wasn't running solo, and took inspiration from her biggest supporter.

Viwe: My father, he was an athlete, back in his days he never got to be a big athlete, a professional athlete, because of where we come from.

Zweledinga: It was that era, you know, the apartheid era. That is what hidden our talents And I was very good.

VO: And it was this proud dad, Zweledinga Jingqi, who traveled to watch Viwe compete in the SA Seniors in April. A daring move by her coach.

Zweledinga: I'm very, very, very much happy. I can say my dream came true.

Claire: So it must have been quite exciting for him. When somebody said that his daughter is talented in running
Viwe: He would go around bragging into like, it's actually my only child that was able to have my genes actually. So whenever he sees me, like he's seeing a vision of him in me.

Zweledinga: I remember the one time I saw her running barefoot in a rubber ground, that's where I was very, very, very much hurt that I started to hunt the spikes for her. I paid one comma five, a pair of Spike. I struggled to to buy because I was not working at that particular moment.

VO: His belief in his daughter was rewarded. In 2019 Viwe was discovered at an SA Schools event, finishing 3rd in the 200 and 400-meter races.

LINK: Viwe was just 14 years old when she received her bursary to TuksSport High School. In this specialized environment, she has the privilege to focus on her sport and her academics

VO: It is through the Athletics Foundation Trust that she received this rare opportunity. Hettie de Villiers has been principal of the school since its inception 20 years ago.

Hettie: 90 learners are in our school and they're are fully sponsored by the trust and they are given an opportunity to come to a good school to get the best coaches, training facilities and just reach their dreams. At the Olympics, we had three boys that came through our school.

Claire: Were you scared, it's a whole new city, it's a whole new way of life.
Viwe: It was horror, you know, coming from villages to the cities, if I may say, it was very, very different. The people the way they do things, the education, so it was just overwhelming.

VO: But with careful guidance from her coach she started to flourish, moving from the 400 meters to the 100 and 200. This mentorship has seen her through deeply troubling times.

LINK: Viwe had a serious emotional setback last year, where her family had to face the tragic loss of her older brother Vukile in a fatal car crash.

Viwe: I think he saw it in me that I have potential so he was more than just a brother to me, but because I'm also very strong, mentally, I was able to get through it. Not easy, but I was able to, like, start (sigh)

Hettie: I think it's very difficult because she's so far away from home. And while we are very close here at the school and she has a support system, that doesn't replace family.

Viwe: So whenever I run, I know my brother is right next to me. When I face the challenges, I know he's fighting with me. So that's one thing I'm just glad of that I had a brother like him

VO: And pushing through her pain - she's made it to head girl, juggling a sports career with matric exams looming. Now she wants to make her mark at the World Juniors in August.

Claire: What is the next big milestone?
Paul: A lot of people has posed the question, should she qualify for World seniors am I sending her and the answer is definitely no.
Claire: Oh?
Paul: Yeah. That is just too much too soon.

VO: Gorries is playing the long game, and he had to make a heartbreaking decision at the SA Senior Championships when Viwe felt a niggle in her hamstring.

Paul: Viwe didn't look too comfortable in the warm-up and I could see there's a little bit of doubt as well. You know, and once there's doubt, and you chip away or no confidence with the sprint, you know, you've already lost 50% there, and I didn't want to take the risk, you know, from a small little niggle to a big injury. So that's why I made the decision to pull her from the race

VO: With her dad waiting on the sidelines the disappointment was palpable.

Zweledinga: I'm disappointed but I'm here. And I will always be here. And I also encourage her not to be disappointed that much because it's part of the sport.

VO: It's this kind of special talent that heralds an Olympic Champion, and with the right support, it could become a reality.

Paul: She could probably be, depending how she developed from now going forward, probably be the best sprinter that ever come out of this country in terms of females.

Claire: South Africans are looking at you for our hopes for Olympics. Does that feel like pressure?
Viwe: To be honest, I like the pressure. It's actually pushing me to running even faster times. But yeah, Olympics are the only things I'm hoping to actually to compete in a few years

Zweledinga: I'm just dreaming of seeing her wearing gold, she's got the ability, she is very strong.
